claims.statement: The authors motivate zero-shot evaluation by the cost of training data: creating a large training corpus is time-consuming and expensive, so many retrieval systems are applied zero-shot.
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: The authors state that it is unclear how well trained neural retrieval models perform on other text domains or tasks, and how sparse versus dense embeddings behave on out-of-distribution data.
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: The authors motivate BEIR by the narrowness of prior evaluation: prior retrieval benchmarks focus on a single task or domain, and neural retrievers have been studied in homogeneous, narrow settings.
confidence_reasons: author statement; characterisation of cited benchmarks not verified
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: According to the BEIR paper, most prior work evaluates neural retrievers on the same dataset they were trained on (for example Natural Questions or MS MARCO), where gains over BM25 are reported.
confidence_reasons: paper's own description of prior work; cited works not read

claims.statement: The BEIR paper describes two earlier benchmarks: MultiReQA (eight question-answering datasets, sentence-level answers, five of eight from Wikipedia, small candidate pools) and KILT (five knowledge-intensive tasks, eleven datasets, retrieval not the primary task, Wikipedia only).
confidence_reasons: paper's own description; cited works not read

claims.statement: Retrieval feeds question answering, claim verification and duplicate-question detection; it has traditionally been dominated by lexical methods such as BM25, which suffer from the lexical gap; the neural families the paper evaluates address this gap in different ways.
confidence_reasons: paper's own summary of background; cited works not read

claims.statement: The authors select BEIR datasets by four factors: diverse tasks, diverse domains, task difficulty (a task solved easily by any algorithm is uninformative for comparing models) and diverse annotation strategies (to reduce the impact of annotation biases).
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: The authors use nDCG@10 as the single metric because it is comparable across tasks: precision and recall are rank-unaware, and MRR and MAP cannot handle graded relevance.
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: MS MARCO scores are reported but excluded from the zero-shot comparison because most evaluated systems were trained on it.
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: Only the first 512 word pieces of each document are used for all neural systems because of the length limits of transformer networks.
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: Baseline settings were chosen empirically: Anserini BM25 because it beat Elasticsearch BM25 and RM3 expansion; default rather than MS-MARCO-tuned BM25 parameters for DeepCT; the DPR Multi model over the NQ-only model; the MiniLM cross-encoder because it was best on MS MARCO among 14 public re-rankers.
confidence_reasons: author statements of design reasons; the comparison runs behind them are not reported
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: Practical constraints shaped some settings: SPARTA was re-implemented because the original code is not public; GenQ was capped at 100K target documents per dataset because of resource constraints; TREC-NEWS and Touche-2020 labels were converted 'for simplicity'.
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: To isolate why TAS-B and ANCE retrieve documents of different lengths, the authors trained two otherwise identical models that differ only in similarity function (cosine versus dot product).
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: During the TREC-COVID re-annotation the annotators did not know which system had retrieved a document, to avoid preference bias.
permitted_verbs: the authors give as their reason

claims.statement: BEIR has 18 English zero-shot datasets from 9 retrieval tasks, ranging from 3.6k to 15M documents, with average query lengths of 3 to 192 words and average document lengths of 11 to 635 words; 8 of the 19 datasets (counting MS MARCO) have training data.
confidence_reasons: counts read from the paper and README table
claims.scope: descriptive statistics of the released benchmark

claims.statement: BEIR supplies a standard data format (corpus, queries, qrels), a Python package (pip install beir) with wrappers for existing retrieval toolkits and IR metrics, and a planned leaderboard; the README lists 17 preprocessed datasets, four of which are not public and come with reproduction instructions.

Ten public systems from five architecture families are evaluated: lexical (BM25), sparse (DeepCT, SPARTA, docT5query), dense (DPR, ANCE, TAS-B, GenQ), late-interaction (ColBERT) and re-ranking (BM25+CE).
confidence_reasons: method details stated in the paper

claims.statement: The authors observe a rather low weighted Jaccard word overlap between datasets from different domains.
confidence_reasons: single similarity measure; heatmap values not recovered from text extraction

claims.statement: The authors read the low cross-domain word overlap as an indication that BEIR is challenging for systems that must handle out-of-distribution domains.
confidence_reasons: authors' inference from a lexical-overlap measure; no direct test of difficulty in the paper

claims.statement: On in-domain MS MARCO, BM25 scores nDCG@10 0.228 and every MS-MARCO-trained neural system scores higher (0.296 to 0.413); the authors describe the gap as 7-18 points. DPR, which was not trained on MS MARCO, scores 0.177.
confidence_reasons: reconstructed Table 2 cells cross-checked with prose

claims.statement: Zero-shot, averaged over the 18 datasets and expressed relative to BM25, BM25+CE is +11%, ColBERT +2.5%, docT5query +1.6%, TAS-B -2.8%, GenQ -3.6%, ANCE -7.4%, SPARTA -20.3%, DeepCT -27.9% and DPR -47.7% (Table 2 last row; the averaging method is not defined in the text).
confidence_reasons: soft evidence: values printed in a damaged table

claims.statement: BM25+CE scores higher than BM25 on 16 of 18 zero-shot datasets and falls below it on exactly two, ArguAna (0.311 vs 0.315) and Touche-2020 (0.271 vs 0.367).
confidence_reasons: count stated in text; two failing scores from reconstructed table

claims.statement: ColBERT scores higher than BM25 on 9 of 18 zero-shot datasets and a bit below the cross-attentional re-ranker.
docT5query scores higher than BM25 on 11 of 18 zero-shot datasets and is competitive on the rest (the text's count is used; the reconstructed Table 2 lists 12).
confidence_reasons: text count chosen over table-derived count

claims.statement: DeepCT and SPARTA, which score well in-domain, score below BM25 on nearly all zero-shot datasets.

Among dense retrievers TAS-B is best zero-shot (higher than ANCE on 14 of 18 datasets and higher than DPR on 17 of 18); dense retrievers fall far below BM25 on some datasets, for example BioASQ (BM25 0.465; TAS-B 0.383; ANCE 0.306; DPR 0.127), and DPR performs worst overall.
confidence_reasons: counts stated in text; per-dataset scores from reconstructed table

claims.statement: TAS-B scores below ANCE on TREC-COVID by 17.3 points and on Touche-2020 by 7.8 points; on TREC-COVID its top-10 documents have a median length of 10 words versus 160 for ANCE, and on Touche-2020 14 versus 89.

In a controlled comparison of two otherwise identical models, switching from cosine similarity to dot product raised TREC-COVID nDCG@10 by 15.3 points (0.482 to 0.635), lowered it on a majority of other datasets (Signal-1M (RT) 0.261 to 0.243), and shifted retrieval toward longer documents.

GenQ (TAS-B further fine-tuned on synthetic queries) scores higher than TAS-B on specialised domains (for example TREC-COVID 0.619 vs 0.481, FiQA-2018 0.308 vs 0.300, CQADupStack 0.347 vs 0.314) and lower on Wikipedia-based datasets (NQ 0.358 vs 0.463, HotpotQA 0.534 vs 0.584); on SCIDOCS it is lower (0.143 vs 0.149).
confidence_reasons: GenQ trained on at most 100K documents per dataset

claims.statement: On 1M DBPedia documents the estimated single-query latency is 450 ms on GPU and 6100 ms on CPU for BM25+CE, 350 ms on GPU for ColBERT, 14 ms on GPU for TAS-B and 20 ms on CPU for BM25; index sizes are 20GB for ColBERT, 12GB for SPARTA, 3GB for dense models and 0.4GB for BM25. For BioASQ (~15M documents) ColBERT needs ~900GB and BM25 18GB.
On TREC-COVID the share of a system's top-10 hits that annotators never judged (Hole@10) is 6.4% for BM25, 2.8% for docT5query, 14.4% for ANCE and 31.8% for TAS-B.

After the authors judged the missing documents, lexical systems changed little (docT5query 0.713 to 0.714) while ANCE rose from 0.654 to 0.735 nDCG@10, 6.7 points above the annotated BM25 score, and ColBERT improved by 5.8 points.
claims.scope: TREC-COVID, nDCG@10 before and after annotating 980 pairs

claims.statement: No single system has the highest zero-shot score on every dataset; BM25 remains a strong baseline, with BM25+CE (16 of 18) the one system scoring above it on nearly all datasets, while the two best systems on average (BM25+CE and ColBERT) are the most costly.

The MS MARCO in-domain ordering of systems does not match their zero-shot ordering (BM25 is last in-domain among MS-MARCO-trained systems yet above most of them zero-shot), which the authors take to mean that in-domain performance does not predict zero-shot performance; the paper gives no correlation statistic.
The authors interpret the strength of re-ranking and late-interaction systems as pointing to cross-attention and cross-attention-like operations as important for out-of-distribution performance.
confidence_reasons: systems also differ in training data and size

claims.statement: The authors explain docT5query's zero-shot strength by document expansion adding new relevant keywords, in contrast to learned term weighting.
The authors speculate that TAS-B's zero-shot strength among dense models comes from its training set-up (in-batch negatives plus Margin-MSE loss with strong teacher models).
confidence_reasons: explicitly labelled speculation by the authors

claims.statement: The authors attribute TAS-B's preference for shorter documents to its loss function; in their controlled experiment the cosine-similarity model preferred shorter documents on all datasets and the dot-product model longer ones, and many TREC-COVID documents are title-only.
confidence_reasons: one controlled experiment with one backbone
alternative causes acknowledged in Appendix H

claims.statement: The best zero-shot systems cost the most: BM25+CE and ColBERT are the slowest and, for ColBERT, have the largest index, while dense retrievers and lexical or sparse methods are faster and lighter.

The BEIR paper states that relevance labels come from pools built by existing systems and that unjudged documents count as irrelevant; it reports lexical bias in some source datasets (BioASQ candidates were retrieved by term matching with boosting tags; 7 of 8 techniques behind Signal-1M (RT) relied on lexical term matching).
confidence_reasons: paper's own description; cited works not read

claims.statement: The authors conclude that the TREC-COVID annotation pool, although built from many systems, still favours lexical approaches and disadvantages non-lexical ones, so part of the dense retrievers' shortfall there reflects missing judgements.
The authors call for datasets built with diverse pooling strategies and note that integrating many systems into BEIR makes creating such pools simpler.
The authors list directions beyond the current benchmark: multilingual and cross-lingual tasks, long-document retrieval, multi-factor and multi-field search, and task-specific models.

The paper asks (i) whether in-domain performance predicts zero-shot performance, (ii) which architectures hold up across heterogeneous datasets, (iii) at what computational cost, and (iv) whether relevance annotation treats non-lexical systems fairly.
confidence_reasons: research questions reconstructed from the authors' framing, not stated as numbered questions

limitations.statement: All BEIR datasets are English, because multilingual retrieval datasets are scarce.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Findings say nothing about other languages or cross-lingual retrieval.

limitations.statement: Most tasks have documents of at most a few hundred words; retrieving longer documents would need a fundamentally different set-up because transformers often have a 512 word-piece limit.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Rankings may differ for long-document retrieval.

limitations.statement: BEIR covers pure text search; real applications also use signals such as PageRank, recency, authority scores or click-through rates, which are hard to integrate.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Text-only rankings may not carry over to multi-signal search.

limitations.statement: Only datasets with one or two text fields are included; multi-field retrieval is not covered.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Results do not speak to retrieval over many fields.

limitations.statement: BEIR evaluates models built to work across tasks; task-specific models can easily beat generic ones and are not what it measures.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The ranking of systems is a ranking of general-purpose systems.

limitations.statement: No benchmark is perfect and has its limitations (the authors' broad statement).
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The central finding holds for this benchmark and these systems, not for retrieval in general.

limitations.statement: No error bars or seed variance are reported, because the systems are existing pre-trained checkpoints that often come without training code and re-training is not feasible.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Differences of a few points between systems cannot be checked against run-to-run variation.

limitations.statement: The total amount of compute used is not reported (only the CPU and GPU types).
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Cost is described by latency and index size only.

limitations.statement: Offensive content and personally identifiable information were not checked in the more than 50 million documents, because removing content would alter the datasets.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Datasets are used as released.

limitations.statement: Potential negative societal impacts of the work are not discussed.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: No societal analysis accompanies the benchmark.

limitations.statement: Even with many systems contributing to the TREC-COVID annotation pool, the pool remains biased towards lexical approaches, which gives non-lexical approaches an unfair disadvantage; fair comparison needs less biased datasets.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Scores of dense and other non-lexical systems on pooled datasets may understate them, so the BM25 comparison is tilted in BM25's favour to an unmeasured degree on most datasets.

limitations.statement: The difference between TAS-B and ANCE is difficult to attribute, because they differ in backbone (DistilBERT vs RoBERTa-base), loss function and hard-negative mining.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The length-preference explanation rests on a separate controlled experiment.

limitations.statement: The maintainers do not vouch for the quality or fairness of the datasets and do not claim that users hold a licence for them; four datasets report no licence.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Users must check licences and dataset quality themselves.

limitations.statement: The annotation-bias study covers one dataset (TREC-COVID) and the nDCG@10 changes concern its top-10 holes; how far lexical bias affects the other 17 datasets is not measured.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The size of the effect elsewhere is unknown; the TREC-COVID result is an existence demonstration for one pool.

limitations.statement: Latency and index size were estimated on one 1M-document DBPedia sample and one CPU/GPU pair.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Absolute numbers will differ on other hardware, corpus sizes and implementations; only the broad ordering is supported.

limitations.statement: Systems differ in several respects at once (training data, backbone, first-stage retrieval): DPR is trained on other data than the MS MARCO systems, and BM25+CE reranks the BM25 top-100.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Differences between systems cannot be assigned to architecture family alone.

limitations.statement: The Table 2 last row averages heterogeneous datasets into one relative number whose computation is not defined; a later study cited by the README (Kamalloo et al., 2024) lists comparisons that reduce heterogeneous scores to a single average as a shortcoming of BEIR comparisons.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Average percentages are a rough summary; per-dataset scores carry the evidence.

limitations.statement: The text's count of datasets where docT5query scores above BM25 (11) differs from the count obtainable from the reconstructed Table 2 (12); the text count is used.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The exact count for docT5query is uncertain by one dataset.

limitations.statement: Several datasets have few test queries (TREC-COVID 50, Touche-2020 49, TREC-NEWS 57, Signal-1M (RT) 97), and per-dataset differences of a few points are reported without intervals.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Small per-dataset differences (for example ArguAna 0.311 vs 0.315) should not be read as reliable orderings.

limitations.statement: SPARTA was re-implemented by the authors and GenQ was capped at 100K documents per dataset, so these two entries may differ from the original or uncapped systems.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Conclusions about these two systems are conclusions about these implementations.

limitations.statement: The missing TREC-COVID judgements were added by the paper's own authors (blind to system), not by independent assessors.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The improved scores rest on the authors' relevance judgements.
